extracted.intended_audience: writers and humorists entering the Bulwer-Lytton Fiction Contest or people studying humorous writing contests
extracted.subtask_description: Compose a deliberately bad opening sentence intended to be the worst possible novel opener; submissions are judged for comedic/egregious poor style and may be placed into category prizes or receive dishonorable mentions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compose the opening sentence to the worst of all possible novels
rubrics_metrics.description: Entrants were invited "to compose the opening sentence to the worst of all possible novels" — that is, one which was deliberately bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The contest specifically asks for an opening sentence (the first line of a novel) that is intentionally bad. The single-sentence requirement and the aim of producing 'the worst' possible novel opener are the core constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberately bad / bad-writing intent
rubrics_metrics.description: Entries should be deliberately bad — written to be amusingly, intentionally poor in quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page emphasizes that submissions are judged on being 'deliberately bad' rather than accidental incompetence; comedic intent and conscious use of bad prose are central to successful entries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single opening sentence format
rubrics_metrics.description: The submission format is the opening sentence (i.e., a single sentence that would open a novel).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The contest centers on the first sentence alone — entrants compose only the opening sentence rather than a paragraph or longer excerpt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Category-specific prizes (detective, romance, Western, purple prose, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: The contest expanded into several subcategories, such as detective fiction, romance novels, Western novels, and purple prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entries could be grouped and judged within genre/category subcompetitions (detective, romance, Western, purple prose), allowing different flavors of 'bad' writing to be recognized. Use of genre tropes to produce hilariously bad openings is acceptable and may qualify an entry for a category prize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dishonorable Mentions for notable but not winning sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences that were notable but not quite bad enough to merit the Grand Prize or a category prize were awarded Dishonorable Mentions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The contest recognizes gradations of merit: beyond grand and category prizes, entries deemed noteworthy for poor quality but not prize-winning receive Dishonorable Mentions — a form of secondary recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemplar / stylistic model: 'It was a dark and stormy night' (purple prose archetype)
rubrics_metrics.description: The contest was named for Edward Bulwer-Lytton, author of the much-quoted first line 'It was a dark and stormy night' (full sentence shown as an example of overwrought opening prose).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The full Paul Clifford sentence is presented as an archetype of florid, overwrought, purple prose — long clauses, melodramatic adjectives, and heavy exposition in the opening line. Entrants often emulate this kind of excess to produce intentionally bad openings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivative variants (Lyttle Lytton Contest: extremely short first sentences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Related/derivative contests exist, e.g., the Lyttle Lytton Contest, which favors extremely short first sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Awareness of derivative formats (such as a variant prize for very short bad openings) indicates alternative judging emphases — extreme brevity rather than purple prose can also be a deliberate strategy for comedic badness.
